title: Universal gravitation
target: Predict how gravitational force changes with mass and separation.
criteria: Apply direct mass and inverse-square distance comparisons.
Identify equal forces on the two interacting bodies.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: Two spherical objects have radii 1 m and 2 m with a 5 m surface gap. Which distance goes into the inverse-square force model?
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A satellite is 300 km above a planet of radius 6,000 km. What is center separation?
cpa.guide: Center distance equals radius plus altitude: 6,000 + 300 = 6,300 km.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Both interacting masses double while separation stays fixed. How does gravitational force change?
cpa.guide: F is proportional to m₁m₂, so the product grows by 4.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Separation triples while masses stay fixed. How does gravitational force change?
options: It becomes nine times as large.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A planet attracts a much smaller moon. Compare their mutual gravitational forces.
options: Only the moon feels a force.
The moon’s force is always zero.
The planet’s force on the moon is larger.
cpa.guide: Newton’s third law applies to the interaction pair.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: Equal mutual forces act on a large planet and a small probe. Why can their accelerations differ greatly?
options: Only the lighter body has inertia.
Equal forces always imply equal acceleration.
The probe feels no real force.
Acceleration is force divided by each body’s mass.
cpa.guide: The smaller mass has larger acceleration under the same force magnitude.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.
